characters: STORY CHARACTERS. Day 1: the old farmer at the frontier (Han China, about 70, thin white topknot and long wispy white beard, weathered brown face, faded indigo hemp robe with rope belt, straw sandals); his son (about 18, black hair tied up, plain undyed hemp tunic and trousers); a dark bay mare with a white blaze; the wild horses are duns and greys. Day 2: Siddhartha before awakening (about 35, South Asian, shaven head with short dark stubble, single unstitched faded ochre cloth over one shoulder, barefoot; when fasting, gaunt but serene, painted respectfully in the tradition of Gandharan art, never grotesque); as a boy (about 7, black hair in a topknot, white cotton cloth, gold bangle); his five companions (wiry ascetics aged 30-50, matted hair, bark-colored cloths). Day 3: the Roman general in triumph (about 45, clean-shaven, laurel wreath, purple-and-gold toga, face painted faintly red); the man behind him (a plain servant, about 30, short dark hair, off-white tunic); Marcus Aurelius (about 55, curly grey-brown hair, full curly grey beard, tired kind eyes, dark red wool military cloak over a plain off-white tunic). Day 4: Shankara (about 25, South Indian, shaven head, three horizontal white ash lines on the forehead, saffron cloth, bamboo staff, brass water pot); his students (young men, shaven heads, saffron and white); the poor man (about 50, dark-skinned, lean, grey stubble, grey hair tied back, rough unbleached waist-cloth and a frayed shoulder cloth, calm direct eyes) with four dogs (rangy pariah dogs: tan, black, white-and-brown, grey). Day 5: Nehemiah (about 40, Judean, short dark beard with grey at the chin, dark curly hair; at court a deep blue Persian robe with gold trim and a white headwrap; later a plain brown traveling cloak); King Artaxerxes (about 50, square curled black beard, tall fluted gold crown, purple robe, seated). Day 6: Jesus (NEVER his face; only from behind, at a distance, or his hands: shoulder-length dark brown hair, undyed cream wool tunic, brown wool mantle, sun-browned working hands); the crowd (Galilean villagers in earth-toned wool, with a recurring mother in a rust headcloth and her son, about 15, tousled black hair); Carl Jung (about 60, 1930s, round wire glasses, white moustache, thinning grey hair, tweed jacket, pipe). Day 7: the Buddha (about 60, South Asian, shaven head, serene face, ochre robe over one shoulder, alms bowl, barefoot), shown respectfully as in traditional art; Angulimala (about 25, big and muscular, wild long black hair and beard, dark rough cloth, iron sword; later shaven-headed in an ochre robe, face softened). TODAY (the last picture of every film, one recurring modern family and friends): Noa (16, light-brown skin, big dark curly hair usually in a high puff, oversized cream hoodie, small gold hoops); her brother Theo (19, buzz cut, short beard shadow, faded denim jacket over a black tee); their mom Dana (about 45, shoulder-length dark hair with a grey streak, olive cardigan, reading glasses pushed up on her head); Noa's best friend Aarav (17, Indian-American, black side-parted hair, round tortoiseshell glasses, navy overshirt). Everyday modern spaces: kitchen, stairs, school cafeteria, bus stop, bedroom. Warm and cool, never corny or posed.

1.story: The old man at the frontier who lost his horse, Huainanzi chapter 18 (Chinese classic, about 139 BCE)
1.point: No one gets told the reason for life's turns, but 'what now?' always has an answer.
1.script: An old Chinese book, the Huainanzi, tells this. A farmer's horse ran off. Bad luck, said the neighbors. The old man said: who knows? Months later, the horse came home, leading fine wild horses. Great luck! Who knows? His son rode one, fell, and broke his leg. Terrible. Who knows? Then war came, and the young men were marched off to fight. The son, with his broken leg, stayed home. Notice what the old man never got: the reason. The book says the turns of luck can't be fully known. People still argue whether there's a plan behind them. But one question always has an answer. Not why. What now?

open.text: the broken leg was the *lucky* part.

1.drop: Notice what the old man never got
pictures: Picture 1: A small mud-walled farm on the windswept northern frontier of Han China at dawn, rolling dry hills and a distant line of watchtowers. The old farmer stands at his wooden gate, hands tucked in his indigo sleeves, the bay mare grazing in a rough pole corral beside him. Soft gold side light, wide establishing shot, quiet and calm.

Picture 2: The bay mare galloping away over a ridge toward the open steppe, dust lifting behind her, a broken corral rail in the foreground. Three neighbors in hemp clothes cluster at the fence shaking their heads; the old farmer stands a little apart, calm, watching. Late afternoon light, long shadows, medium-wide.

Picture 3: Months later, the bay mare trotting back down the hill toward the farm, leading three magnificent wild horses, duns and greys with flowing manes. The neighbors point and cheer; the son runs out, delighted. The old farmer stands at the gate, one eyebrow raised, unmoved. Bright clear morning, wide shot.

Picture 4: The son thrown from a rearing grey wild horse in a dusty field, caught mid-fall, arms out, the horse twisting away. No injury shown. The old farmer in the background mid-step, starting toward him. Dynamic diagonal composition, warm dust in the air, no blood.

Picture 5: A column of young men in padded tunics with bows and spears marching away down the dirt road under grey skies, a plain banner with no writing snapping in the wind. In the foreground, the son sits on the farmhouse step, leg splinted with wooden slats and cloth, a crutch beside him; the old farmer's hand rests on his shoulder. Both watch the column go. Muted light, a single warm glow from the doorway behind them.

Picture 6: TODAY. Modern family, warm painterly realism (same art style as the story pictures, contemporary setting): Noa sits on the bottom stair at home in her cream hoodie, phone face-down on her knee after bad news (a rejection, a plan fallen through), eyes red but steady. Theo sits down beside her holding two mugs and hands her one; their mom Dana is visible in the warm kitchen doorway behind. Evening lamp light, close and tender, cool not corny.
motion: Slow push in toward the farmer at the gate as wind ripples the dry grass and his sleeves.
Camera holds wide while the mare gallops away over the ridge and dust drifts toward the lens.
Slow pan following the horses down the hill as their manes stream and the neighbors raise their arms.
Slight slow-motion feel: the horse twists away and dust swirls while the camera eases sideways.
The column marches slowly out of frame as the banner flutters and the camera pulls back from the father and son on the step.
Gentle push in as Theo hands Noa the mug and steam curls up between them.

2.story: The Buddha gives up starving and breathless meditation and remembers the rose-apple tree, Majjhima Nikaya 36 (Mahasaccaka Sutta), Pali Canon; his breath practice per Samyutta Nikaya 54.8 (Buddhist)
2.point: Meditation isn't forcing a blank mind; it's feeling the breath, wandering, noticing and coming back.
2.script: Before he was the Buddha, he was a prince who gave up everything to find the truth. He starved himself to skin and bone. He even tried to stop breathing, until his head pounded like a drum. Nothing. Then he remembered something. As a boy, sitting in the shade of a rose-apple tree, he'd felt a calm that came on its own. No forcing. So he ate a bowl of rice. His five companions walked out in disgust. He's quit, they said. He hadn't. He'd found the way in. Buddhists still begin where he did: with the breath. Feel it. Wander. Notice. Come back. Your mind wanders twenty times in a minute? That's twenty reps.
pictures: Picture 1: The young prince Siddhartha, in fine white and gold, walks away from a lamplit palace gate at night toward a dark forest, his jeweled turban held loosely at his side. Moonlight and torchlight, seen from the side, wide and quiet. Respectful traditional Buddhist art register.

Picture 2: Deep in a forest grove, Siddhartha sits cross-legged, gaunt from fasting, painted respectfully in the style of Gandharan fasting-Buddha sculpture, eyes squeezed shut, lips sealed as he holds his breath, a strained stillness. His five companions sit around him in a ring, watching in awe. Harsh noon light through leaves.

Picture 3: Memory scene in a warmer, softer palette: the boy Siddhartha, about 7, sits peacefully in the cool shade of a large rose-apple tree at the edge of a field, eyes half closed, a small smile, while in the sunny distance farmers and oxen work the field. Dappled gold light, dreamy edges.

Picture 4: By a riverbank at the forest's edge, the gaunt Siddhartha, seated, accepts a simple clay bowl of boiled rice and milk porridge from the hands of a village woman (seen from behind, at the edge of frame). Soft morning light, steam rising from the bowl, gentle and dignified.

Picture 5: The five companions, backs turned, walk away down a forest path in a line, one glancing back with a scowl. In the background, small, Siddhartha sits calmly under a tree with the empty bowl beside him, untroubled. Late afternoon light, long shadows, wide shot.

Picture 6: TODAY. Modern family, warm painterly realism (same art style as the story pictures, contemporary setting): Noa sits cross-legged on her bedroom floor by the window in her cream hoodie, eyes closed, one hand on her belly, a small smile because her mind just wandered and she noticed. On the bed behind her, Aarav sits the same way, peeking one eye open at her. Soft morning light, plants on the sill, a phone timer glowing face-up on the rug (no readable text).
motion: Slow tracking shot as he walks from the torchlit gate into the dark trees, his cloth moving.
Very slow push in on his still face as leaves tremble overhead and light flickers across the ring of companions.
Leaves of the rose-apple tree sway softly while the camera drifts in on the boy's calm face.
Steam curls from the bowl as the camera slowly lifts from the woman's hands to his face.
The companions walk away down the path while the camera holds still on the calm seated figure.
Gentle push in on Noa as her chest rises with one long breath and the curtain light shifts.

3.story: The Roman triumph's reminder (Tertullian, Apologeticum 33) and Marcus Aurelius on death in the Meditations (4.17), Roman Stoic philosophy
3.point: Memento mori means remembering that you will die so that you live well now, not so that you live in fear.
3.script: In ancient Rome, a winning general rode through the city in a golden chariot. Crowds roared his name. And, an old writer says, a voice behind him kept saying: look behind you. Remember you're only human. One emperor gave himself that reminder. Marcus Aurelius, ruler of the whole Roman world, sat in an army tent by lamplight, writing private notes about death. Again and again. You'd expect fear. It isn't there. Don't act as if you'll live ten thousand years, he wrote. While you live, while you can, be good. That's memento mori. Remember you will die, so today comes clear. The apology you keep saving for next month? It's this month's.
pictures: Picture 1: A Roman triumph through a sunlit marble street: the general in purple and gold with a laurel wreath stands in a gilded four-horse chariot, crowds packed on steps and balconies throwing flower petals, white horses with plumes. Bright midday light, low angle, wide and loud.

Picture 2: Close on the chariot from behind: a plain servant in an off-white tunic stands just behind the general, leaning close to his ear and holding a golden wreath above his head, while the general stares ahead at the roaring crowd, a flicker of unease on his face. Warm light, petals in the air.

Picture 3: Night in a Roman army camp on the cold Danube frontier: rows of leather tents, a few campfires, mist on the dark river. One tent glows from inside. Cool blue moonlight against warm amber lamp glow, wide establishing shot.

Picture 4: Inside the tent, Marcus Aurelius sits at a simple wooden camp table in his dark red cloak, writing with a reed pen on a scroll by a single oil lamp (only soft, unreadable marks, no letters). His face is calm, tired and thoughtful, not afraid. Close medium shot, deep shadows, golden lamplight.

Picture 5: Dawn: Marcus steps out of the tent flap in his red cloak, looking out over the camp waking up, soldiers lighting fires, the river turning pink. He stands still, as if deciding how to spend the day. Soft rose-gold light, medium-wide from behind and to the side.

Picture 6: TODAY. Modern family, warm painterly realism (same art style as the story pictures, contemporary setting): Theo, in his denim jacket, stands on a friend's front porch at golden hour; the door opens and the friend, his age, in a hoodie, looks surprised, then softens. Theo holds out two iced coffees with a sheepish half-smile: the apology he finally came to make. Noa watches from the car at the curb, grinning. Warm late light.
motion: Low tracking shot alongside the chariot as petals rain down and the horses' plumes bob.
Slow push in over the servant's shoulder toward the general's uneasy face as petals drift past.
Mist drifts slowly over the river while the camera eases toward the one glowing tent.
The lamp flame flickers and the reed pen moves as the camera inches closer to his face.
Smoke rises from waking fires and the camera slowly rises past Marcus to reveal the dawn river.
The door swings open and the camera gently pushes in on the friend's softening face.

4.story: Shankara and the man with four dogs at Varanasi, the traditional framing story of the Manisha Panchakam (Hindu tradition, attributed to Adi Shankara)
4.point: Namaste means 'a bow to you', and the bow is meant for the person themselves, whatever their rank.
4.script: Hindu tradition tells this story. At dawn in Varanasi, a young teacher named Shankara walked down to the river Ganga. On the steps stood a poor man with four dogs, a man his society called untouchable. Move aside, Shankara said. The man didn't move. He asked: move what? This body, made of food, away from yours, made of food? Or the awareness in me, away from the awareness in you? It's the same. Shankara stopped. And bowed to him. Many Hindus hear that bow inside namaste. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. Not to someone's rank, or money, or mood. To them. So mean it. Even to the kid nobody sits with.
pictures: Picture 1: Dawn over the stone ghats of Varanasi: wide steps descending to the misty river Ganga, temple spires along the bank, small oil lamps floating on the water, boats in the haze. Shankara in saffron with his staff and brass pot walks down the steps with three students behind him. Peach and gold light, wide establishing shot, sacred art register.

Picture 2: Halfway down the steps, the poor man stands in the path with his four rangy dogs around his feet, calm and still, his frayed cloth over one shoulder. Seen from Shankara's side, slightly low angle on the man, river mist behind him. Soft warm light, medium shot.

Picture 3: Shankara raises one hand, palm out, gesturing the man aside; his students frown behind him. The man does not move; one dog sits down. Tension in the composition, the river glowing between them. Medium-wide, side view.

Picture 4: Close on the poor man's face, calm, kind and piercing, as he answers; behind him the rising sun turns the river gold, and the sun's reflection shimmers in a small puddle on the step at his feet. Shallow depth, warm rim light on his grey stubble.

Picture 5: Shankara, staff set down on the step, bows low before the man with palms pressed together, his students stunned behind him; the man looks down at him gently, dogs at his side. Golden sunrise flooding the ghat, wide and reverent.

Picture 6: TODAY. Modern family, warm painterly realism (same art style as the story pictures, contemporary setting): A school cafeteria at lunch. Noa and Aarav, trays in hand, stop at a table where a new kid sits alone with earbuds in; Aarav gives a small, easy palms-together nod and Noa slides in beside the kid, who looks up, surprised and starting to smile. Bright natural light, real teen clothes, warm not staged.
motion: Slow drift down the steps toward the river as lamps bob on the water and mist moves.
Camera eases closer to the man and his dogs as one dog's ears twitch and his cloth stirs.
Slight push across the gap between them as Shankara's hand rises and the river shimmers.
Very slow push in on the man's face as sunlight brightens on the water behind him.
Camera slowly rises and pulls back as Shankara bows and sunlight spreads over the ghat.
Gentle push in as the new kid pulls out an earbud and starts to smile.

5.story: Nehemiah inspects Jerusalem's broken walls by night and rebuilds them, Book of Nehemiah 1-6 (Hebrew Bible)
5.point: Wishing alone isn't enough; what works is picturing the wish, then honestly facing what's in the way and planning for it.
5.script: In the Hebrew Bible, a man named Nehemiah poured wine for the king of Persia. Then news came: back home, Jerusalem's walls lay broken, its gates burned. He wept. He prayed. Then he did something most dreamers skip. He traveled to the city, rode out at night, and inspected every broken stretch of wall. Only then did he gather the people and make a plan: families rebuilt the sections near their own homes. When enemies threatened, the Bible says, they prayed, and set a guard. The wall rose in fifty-two days. Manifesting is new: 1800s America. But this old story knew its missing half. Picture the wish. Then walk the wall.

open.text: he walked the *broken wall* at night.

5.drop: Then he did something most dreamers skip.
pictures: Picture 1: The Persian palace at Susa: tall carved stone columns with bull capitals, rich hangings, King Artaxerxes seated on a throne. Nehemiah, in his blue court robe, stands at his side pouring wine from a gold pitcher into the king's cup. Warm torchlight and gold, wide and grand.

Picture 2: A palace courtyard at dusk: dusty travelers in worn cloaks have just arrived and speak urgently; Nehemiah sits on a low stone bench, head in his hands, grief on his face, his blue robe pooled around him. Soft violet evening light, medium shot.

Picture 3: Night outside Jerusalem: Nehemiah, in a brown traveling cloak, rides a single grey donkey slowly along the rubble of the broken city wall, two companions on foot with a small lantern behind him. Collapsed stones, charred gate timbers, a huge starry sky. Deep blue night with a warm lantern pool, wide shot.

Picture 4: Morning inside the city: Nehemiah stands on a heap of stones, pointing along the wall, surrounded by families of builders, men, women and teenagers with baskets, mortar and ropes, each group taking a stretch of wall beside their own houses. Bright clear morning, busy, hopeful, wide.

Picture 5: Night on the half-built wall: builders set the last stones of the day while a line of watchmen with torches stand guard along the top, calm and alert; a few people sit with heads bowed in quiet prayer by a fire. Warm firelight against a dark sky, no fighting, medium-wide. Nothing divine is depicted.

Picture 6: TODAY. Modern family, warm painterly realism (same art style as the story pictures, contemporary setting): Noa's bedroom: Noa and Theo stand in front of a big corkboard. On the left, a vision board of photos and cut-out pictures; on the right, Noa is pinning sticky notes into a second column, the hard part (a work-shift calendar, a crowded week), while Theo points at one, helping her plan. No readable words anywhere. Warm desk-lamp light, real and lived-in.
motion: Wine pours in a glinting stream as torchlight flickers and the camera eases slowly toward the throne.
Camera slowly pushes in on Nehemiah's bowed head as the travelers' cloaks shift in the evening breeze.
The donkey plods steadily along the rubble as the lantern sways and the camera tracks alongside.
Camera rises up past Nehemiah to reveal builders spreading out along the wall, baskets moving.
Torch flames flicker along the wall while the camera slowly pans along the line of watchmen.
Noa presses a sticky note onto the board and the camera gently pulls back to show both columns.

6.story: The speck and the plank, the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 7:3-5 (Christian Gospels), with Carl Jung's idea of the shadow
6.point: What annoys us most in other people can point to something unclaimed in ourselves, what Jung called the shadow.
6.script: In the Gospel of Matthew, a crowd sits on a hillside in Galilee, listening to Jesus. People knew him as a carpenter. And he hands them a carpenter's picture. Why do you look at the speck in your brother's eye, he asks, and miss the plank in your own? Picture it. A man with a whole beam of wood sticking out of his eye, squinting, trying to pick a splinter out of his friend's. It's funny. Then it isn't. Centuries later, the psychiatrist Carl Jung named the pattern: the shadow. What we won't own in ourselves, we spot in everyone else. So when someone bugs you more than they should, ask: is any of this mine?

open.text: a man with a *plank* in his eye.

pictures: Picture 1: A green hillside above the Sea of Galilee in spring, wildflowers, a large crowd of villagers in earth-toned wool seated on the slope. Jesus is seen only from behind and at a distance, standing slightly below them near a rock, brown mantle and shoulder-length dark hair, one hand raised mid-teaching. Late morning light, blue lake beyond, wide shot. His face is never shown.

Picture 2: Close on working hands only: sun-browned hands running a wooden hand plane along a beam in a simple stone workshop, curls of wood shavings and a fine drift of sawdust in a shaft of light. No face. Warm amber light, shallow depth.

Picture 3: Faces in the crowd listening: the mother in a rust headcloth and her teenage son exchange a guilty sideways glance and a smile, an old man nearby rubs his chin; far in the soft background, the teacher is a small figure seen from behind. Soft daylight, medium close.

Picture 4: A gently comic, painterly vision: a Galilean man with a huge wooden beam absurdly sticking out from his eye, squinting with great concentration as he carefully reaches to pick a tiny splinter from his patient friend's eye; the end of the beam is about to knock over a water jar. Bright warm light, humorous, no injury, no blood, playful exaggeration within the painterly style.

Picture 5: Zurich, 1930s: Carl Jung in tweed and round glasses sits in a book-lined study by a lake window, pipe in hand, listening thoughtfully to a patient in an armchair whose shadow on the wall behind is larger and a different shape. Book spines without readable titles. Soft grey lake light and a warm lamp.

Picture 6: TODAY. Modern family, warm painterly realism (same art style as the story pictures, contemporary setting): Noa at her desk after school, in her cream hoodie, about to fire off an annoyed text about a classmate, then pausing, thumb hovering, catching her own reflection in the dark window beside her. Dana leans in the doorway with a knowing, gentle look. Evening light, desk lamp, real and wry. Phone screen shows no readable text.
motion: Slow push over the seated crowd toward the distant figure as wildflowers and hair stir in the breeze.
The plane slides along the beam and wood shavings curl and fall through the light.
Camera drifts slowly across the listening faces as the mother and son glance at each other.
The beam wobbles as the man leans in and the water jar tips slightly while the camera nudges closer.
Pipe smoke curls upward as the camera slowly moves past Jung to the large shadow on the wall.
Noa's thumb stops above the screen and the camera eases toward her reflection in the window.

7.story: The Buddha and the bandit Angulimala, Majjhima Nikaya 86 (Angulimala Sutta), Pali Canon; 'intention is karma', Anguttara Nikaya 6.63 (Buddhist)
7.point: Karma means action, and the Buddha said the intention behind it is what counts, so karma is about what you are planting, not payback for others.
7.script: In the Buddha's time, a bandit named Angulimala terrified the forests of Kosala. Whole villages emptied. One morning, the Buddha walked straight down his road, alone. Angulimala grabbed his sword and ran after him. But however fast he ran, he couldn't catch a man who was only walking. Stop, monk! he shouted. The Buddha said: I have stopped. It's you who hasn't. That landed. Angulimala threw down his sword, and became a monk. The Buddha taught that karma isn't payback. It's action. And, he said, intention is what I call karma. The choice is the seed. So when a friend texts karma! about someone else, flip it. What am I planting, right now?

open.text: he ran, but couldn't catch *a walker.*

pictures: Picture 1: A deep dark forest in ancient Kosala, tangled sal trees and hanging vines; at its edge, a small village of thatched huts stands empty, a cart abandoned, a goat wandering alone. Deep in the trees, the silhouette of a big wild-haired man watches. Grey-green gloom, ominous but not violent, wide shot.

Picture 2: Morning: the Buddha, in his ochre robe with alms bowl, walks calmly alone down a dusty forest road into the trees, while cowherds and farmers at the roadside wave their arms, warning him to turn back. Soft golden light, respectful traditional depiction, wide.

Picture 3: Angulimala, wild hair and beard flying, sword in hand, sprinting hard down the road in a burst of dust, straining every muscle; ahead, the Buddha walks at an easy, steady pace, robe barely moving, the distance between them impossibly unchanged. Dramatic low angle, dappled light, motion against stillness. No blood.

Picture 4: Angulimala has stopped, panting, sword lowered, shouting; the Buddha has turned to face him, serene, one hand raised in the traditional gesture of fearlessness. A shaft of sunlight falls between them through the canopy. Medium shot, intense and quiet.

Picture 5: The sword lies dropped on the forest floor among leaves; beyond it, Angulimala, now shaven-headed in an ochre robe, kneels with palms together before the Buddha, his face softened. Warm light breaking through the trees. Medium-wide, peaceful.

Picture 6: Under a large tree, the Buddha sits teaching a small circle of monks, Angulimala among them; in the foreground, a monk's open palm holds a single small seed, in sharp focus. Soft afternoon light, sacred art register.

Picture 7: TODAY. Modern family, warm painterly realism (same art style as the story pictures, contemporary setting): Theo and Aarav at a bus stop; Aarav's phone lights up (no readable text) and he laughs, about to reply, while Theo, noticing a stressed classmate nearby who just dropped her books, crouches to help her pick them up. Aarav's grin turns thoughtful. Late afternoon city light, warm and real.
motion: Slow push into the dark forest past the empty village as vines sway and the goat wanders.
Camera tracks behind the Buddha as he walks on and the villagers' arms wave in the background.
Angulimala's hair and dust fly while the Buddha's robe barely moves as the camera holds the gap between them.
The sunbeam brightens between them and dust settles as the camera slowly pushes in.
Leaves drift down onto the dropped sword as the camera rises toward the kneeling monk.
Very slow push in on the seed in the open palm while leaves stir overhead.
Theo crouches to gather the books as the camera eases in on Aarav's changing face.

sources_check: Day 1: Huainanzi 18 (the old man at the frontier who lost his horse); lesson sources Kelemen 1999 and Banerjee & Bloom 2014 for the 'what now' frame

Day 2: Majjhima Nikaya 36 (Mahasaccaka Sutta: austerities, breathless meditation, the rose-apple tree memory, eating boiled rice and porridge, the five companions leave); Samyutta Nikaya 54.8 (before awakening he mostly dwelt in mindfulness of breathing); William James, Principles of Psychology ch. XI

Day 3: Tertullian, Apologeticum 33 ('look behind you, remember you are a man'); Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.17 (Long 1862, paraphrased in modern English); camp setting from the Meditations' book headings (among the Quadi, at Carnuntum)
Day 4: Manisha Panchakam (attributed to Adi Shankara) and its traditional framing story at Varanasi; Monier-Williams for namas / te

Day 5: Nehemiah 1:1-4 (cupbearer; broken walls, burned gates; weeps and prays), 2:1-15 (asks the king; inspects the walls by night), 3 (builders repair sections, some opposite their own houses), 4:9 (prayed and set a watch day and night), 6:15 (finished in fifty-two days); lesson's New Thought and Oettingen sources for 'manifesting is new'
Day 6: Matthew 7:3-5 (speck and beam); Mark 6:3 ('is not this the carpenter'); C. G. Jung, Aion ch. 2 'The Shadow' (paraphrased)

Day 7: Majjhima Nikaya 86 (Angulimala Sutta: villages emptied, the Buddha walks his road, cannot be caught, 'I have stopped, you stop too', throws away his weapons, ordains); Anguttara Nikaya 6.63 (intention is kamma)
risks: Day 1: 'who knows?' paraphrases the old man's repeated 'how do you know this isn't good fortune / misfortune?'. The Huainanzi adds that most of the young men died in the war; the film leaves that out.

Day 2: 'head pounded like a drum' softens MN 36's images (a sword splitting the head, a strap tightened round it). 'Buddhists still begin where he did: with the breath' leans on SN 54.8 and later tradition that he used breath meditation on the night of awakening; not every school starts with the breath. The woman who brings food is from later tradition (Sujata), not MN 36, so she is not named or shown in full.

Day 3: Tertullian is the only real source for the triumph reminder, and his words are 'remember you are a man', not 'memento mori'; the film avoids claiming the whisper was 'memento mori'. Historians debate how standard the custom was. The lamplit army tent is an inference from the Meditations' camp headings, not a scene the text describes.

Day 4: the Shankara story is the traditional framing of the Manisha Panchakam, not documented history; some tellings make the man Shiva in disguise and the dogs the four Vedas (the film says neither). 'Untouchable' is historically accurate but painful; a scholar and a Dalit reader should check the wording. 'Many Hindus hear that bow inside namaste' ties an Advaita story to an everyday greeting, which is an interpretation; it stays consistent with the lesson's point that the 'light in me' line is a modern reading.

Day 5: Nehemiah is not in the lesson's own sources; it was chosen to give 'picture the wish, then the wall' a real old story. The film keeps the lesson's point that manifesting is modern (1800s America). 'Families rebuilt the sections near their own homes' simplifies Nehemiah 3 (many groups, some 'opposite their house'). God is not depicted or quoted.

Day 6: the carpenter link is the narrator's observation, not something the Gospel says. Matthew 7 is paraphrased, not quoted. Jesus' face is never shown (behind, distance, hands only). Jung is paraphrased because his works are under copyright; check that the comic 'plank in the eye' picture reads as playful, not as an injury.

Day 7: 'I have stopped. It's you who hasn't' paraphrases MN 86 ('I have stopped, Angulimala; you stop too'). His name means 'garland of fingers'; script and pictures deliberately leave that out (no gore). The Buddha is depicted, which the brief allows; painters should follow traditional, respectful conventions (calm face, ochre robe, no caricature).

General: this path is cross-faith on purpose; each film credits one tradition plainly (a Chinese classic, Buddhist, Roman Stoic, Hindu, Hebrew Bible, Christian Gospel, Buddhist).
